svg.text: Confidentiality: the rule, and the four doors out of it
The duty survives discharge, and it survives death.
The rule
Information obtained about a patient is not disclosed to anyone without that patient's consent.
Patients' Charter, right 8. This includes family, employers, colleagues not involved in the care, and the patient's church.
Door 1 — the patient agrees
Consent to share, ideally recorded.
Ask who may be told, and what.
A relative in the waiting room is
not automatically entitled to know.
Door 2 — the care team needs it
Share on a need-to-know basis.
The colleague taking over the
patient needs the handover. The
colleague who is curious does not.
Door 3 — the law requires it
Notifiable disease, court order,
statutory reporting duty.
A police officer asking informally
is not a court order.
Door 4 — serious risk to others
Disclosure in the public interest,
limited to what is necessary.
Tell the patient first where you
safely can, and tell the right
person, not everyone.
Where nurses actually breach it, without meaning to
• Discussing a patient in the corridor, the canteen, the trotro or the staff WhatsApp group.
• Posting a photograph from the ward. A patient can be identified by a wristband, a bedsheet, a tattoo or a room.
• Looking up the record of a neighbour, a relative or a colleague out of concern. Access is not the same as authority.
• Telling a husband his wife's diagnosis because he asked and he is paying the bill.
Removing the name is not enough. If the person can still be worked out, it is still a breach.
